#10093. Harness, Scaffold, and the AI Agent Terms Worth Getting Right

When a field evolves quickly, its vocabulary often evolves faster than its shared understanding. Terms start to blur, get reused in different contexts, or become shorthand for ideas that are never fully explained. We are currently seeing this happen in the field of AI Agents, where concepts are getting mixed together, some are renamed, and others are widely used for a few months before quietly disappearing.

This can be overwhelming for newcomers, and even for practitioners trying to keep up with the latest developments. After ICLR 2026, one of us (@ariG23498) posted a question that captured this confusion well:

"What do you mean by the terms 'harness' and 'scaffold' in the context of agents? I have heard a lot of explanations while I was at ICLR, but I could not understand why they did not converge to a single explanation."

This glossary is our attempt to ground the terms that keep coming up without clear, consistent explanations. It is not meant to be a comprehensive dictionary of every term in the field. Instead, we focus on the concepts that are often mixed up, reused in different ways, or assumed to be obvious when they are not.

Most of these terms come up whether you're building an agent, deploying one, or just using tools like Claude Code, Codex, or Hermes Agent. The last section covers concepts specific to training models, which is more relevant if you work on that side of things.

Many of these terms don't have universally accepted definitions yet, and different frameworks use the same word differently. The goal here is not to enforce one correct vocabulary, but to provide a practical mental model that makes discussions easier to follow.

The model is the LLM: it takes text in and produces text out (e.g., Claude, Qwen, GPT, Kimi, DeepSeek…). On its own, it has no memory between calls, and no loop. The model can express the intent to call a tool, but it needs a harness to actually execute it. It answers one prompt and stops. Wrap it in scaffolding and a harness and it becomes an agent.

The behavior-defining layer around the model: system prompt, tool descriptions, how the model's responses get parsed, what it remembers across steps (context management). It shapes how the model sees the world and acts in it, whether during training or at inference.

Products like Claude Code, Codex, and Antigravity CLI call the whole thing a harness. Claude Code's own docs say it directly: "Claude Code serves as the agentic harness around Claude." That's the broad use: harness means everything that isn't the model. The scaffold/harness distinction matters most when you need to reason about them separately, as in a training pipeline. You'll also hear "scaffold" used more broadly to cover any infrastructure the harness relies on: hooks, runtime configuration, even directory structure.

Some products like Claude Code and Codex are tightly coupled to their provider's models. Others like Antigravity CLI and Hermes Agent let you plug in any model.

The execution layer inside the agent: it calls the model, handles its tool calls, decides when to stop. The harness is what makes the agent run. Scaffolding, defined above, is what the model works from: its instructions, its tools, its format.

Harness engineering is the discipline of designing this layer well: deciding when the agent should stop, how errors get handled, and what guardrails keep it on track. It applies at both training and inference. Addy Osmani's piece and OpenAI's account of building with Codex both cover this from the inference side.

At evaluation time, the same pattern shows up as an eval harness: instead of collecting training data, it runs a fixed set of scenarios at a model checkpoint and records metrics rather than updating weights.

Some frameworks use orchestrator for a higher-level controller that coordinates work across multiple agents. Unlike a harness, which drives a model through its execution loop, an orchestrator manages agents as units, each running their own harness (see Sub-agents below).

The term comes from reinforcement learning, where an agent is simply a function that takes an observation and returns an action. The environment takes that action and returns a new observation, and the loop repeats. That loop is still at the core of how LLM agents work.

In the LLM world, the term has expanded. An agent is a model plus everything around it that lets it act, not just respond. It turns raw text generation into something that can act in a loop: taking in information, deciding what to do, and acting on the results.

Take a coding agent as a concrete example. The system prompt, tool descriptions, and the output format the model follows form the scaffolding. The loop that calls the model, handles its tool calls, and decides when to stop is the harness. At training time, the harness also runs many of these loops in parallel and feeds the results back to update the model.

In the community, it's usually put as Agent = Model + Harness (@Vtrivedy10 and Will Brown's tweet for reference). If you're not the model, you're the harness. The subtle distinction between harness and scaffold that creates most of the confusion is what the two sections above address.

When people talk about products like Claude Code, Codex, or Cursor, they're referring to a specific harness built on top of a specific model, designed and optimized together. Two products using the same underlying model can feel completely different because their harnesses make different choices. And swapping a better model into the same harness also changes the experience. The model, the harness, and the product are three different things.

Designing what goes into the agent's context window: what the model sees at each step, system prompt, tool descriptions, conversation history, retrieved knowledge. It's not a one-time decision: as the model runs, previous turns shape what goes into future calls, and the harness actively manages this throughout the run. It applies at both training and inference, but the cost of getting it wrong is very different. At training, what the model sees shapes what gets learned. Get it wrong and you're retraining. At inference, it's just text: change a prompt and redeploy. The HF Context Engineering Course covers this in depth.

Memory is part of this picture. Short-term memory is what stays in the context window during a single run: conversation history, tool results, previous reasoning. Long-term memory persists across sessions, stored externally and retrieved on demand, then injected back into context when relevant.

A policy is the behavior an agent follows: given any situation, it defines the probability of taking each possible action. In LLM systems, part of that policy is learned in the model weights, but the behavior also depends on the surrounding scaffolding and harness. The same model can behave very differently depending on its prompts, tools, memory, and execution loop.

A policy is not an agent. The policy defines behavior; the agent is the full system that acts in an environment. Wrap a checkpoint in scaffolding and a harness and deploy it, and you get an agent whose behavior is the policy.

How agents reach outside themselves: APIs, code interpreters, databases, web search, file systems. The model expresses the intent to use a tool in a structured format. Modern inference APIs surface this as a first-class object: the harness receives the call directly and routes it to the right function. The result gets fed back into context and the loop continues.

Reusable, structured packages of knowledge that enable multi-step tasks. Where a tool is an action ("run this command"), a skill bundles everything needed to accomplish a goal ("investigate this bug, form a hypothesis, write a fix"). They are portable across agents and loaded on demand. The line between tool, skill, and sub-agent shifts across frameworks. The HF Context Engineering Course covers skills in depth.

An agent called by another agent to handle a specific subtask. It has its own model and scaffold, reasons independently, and returns a result. The calling agent doesn't need to know how it works internally. This is what separates a sub-agent from a tool (a function call) or a skill (packaged knowledge): a sub-agent can itself reason, use tools, and call further sub-agents. The calling agent is sometimes called an orchestrator.

The terms above apply whether you're training or deploying. These four are specific to training, where the agent runs through tasks, gets scored, and its model's weights get updated. Every RL training system for LLMs is built around the same pipeline:

The environment is anything you can interact with: a stateful object that takes an action as input, updates its internal state, and returns an observation. In the LLM context, actions are typically tool calls. A filesystem is a simple example: the action touch foo.txt updates the state by creating the file, and the observation might be the updated file listing. Definitions vary across frameworks.

We recently published a dedicated guide on this, so rather than compress it here, see The Ultimate Guide to RL Environments for a complete breakdown of types, frameworks, and examples.

The trainer is what makes the agent better: it runs many agent episodes, scores the results and uses them to update the inner model's weights. TRL's GRPOTrainer is a concrete example: a single class that handles episode generation, reward scoring, and weight updates.

A rollout is one full agent run from start to finish: what the agent saw, what it did, and what reward it got at each step. It's also called a trajectory or a trace, depending on the context. This is the raw data RL algorithms learn from.

The score that tells the training algorithm whether the model is getting better. It can be verifiable (tests pass/fail, answer matches), or learned (human preferences, LLM-as-judge), sparse (one score at the end of an episode), or dense (a score at each step). This is what the trainer uses to actually update the inner model's weights. For a thorough breakdown of each type, see the Reward Architecture section in Adithya's guide.

Rubrics break the reward into explicit dimensions with weights, rather than a single number. OpenEnv and Verifiers implement rubrics as objects you can combine (WeightedSum, Sequential, Gate).

If any definition feels imprecise or you've encountered a term we've missed, we'd love to hear from you.

Thanks to Pedro Cuenca, Quentin Gallouédec, Shaun Smith, and Adithya S Kolavi for reviewing this post.

The definition of Agent in popular use changes every year :)

We really leaned into Autonomy in this post from last year, but this year it seems to be all about model + harnesses: https://huggingface.co/blog/ethics-soc-7

All in all, the more precise and technically specific the term, the better!

Coding Agent, or Agent CLI – a command-line application, used to launch and manage agent instances (e.g. Opencode, Claude Code, Copilot CLI, Gemini CLI, etc)

Agent Definition – a file (Markdown/JSON) that describes how an agent behaves; serves as a blueprint from which instances are created (like a class in Java)

Agent Instance – a running process created from an Agent Definition (like an object instantiated from a class in Java).

Agent / AI Agent – avoid; use the specific term (CLI, Definition, or Instance) depending on what you mean; not to forget that “Agent” can also mean the CI pipeline agent or a human agent

it's a standardization protocol that makes the Tool Use → Harness connection much cleaner and more interoperable. The glossary describes what agents do; MCP is a specification for how they do the tool-calling part reliably across different vendors and implementations.

Appreciate the nice writeup. Can we add a) Leaderboard, b) Benchmark

Really useful glossary, and I especially appreciate the attempt to separate the model, harness, scaffold, tools, context, and training loop.

One concern I have is with standardizing on “scaffolding” as the term for the behavior-defining layer around the model. To me, “scaffolding” already feels quite overloaded, specifically in software projects. It is used extensively in code generation, and more narrowly by framework generators to create routes, controllers, models, migrations, components, tests, and other boilerplate structures.

I wonder whether “rigging” might be a better candidate. It still relates naturally to the metaphor of a harness, but is less already-standardized in adjacent software and AI contexts. In the horse/cart sense, rigging is the arrangement that attaches the harness to the thing being pulled and makes the whole setup usable. That feels close to what this layer does for an agent: system prompt, tool descriptions, response formats, memory/context rules, and other configurations that connect the model to the operational environment in a particular way.

#10090. Build Live Video Chat With WebRTC: From First Call to Production Debugging

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

Adding real-time video to a web app used to mean plugins, proprietary SDKs and a lot of money. Today every modern browser ships with WebRTC, a set of APIs that lets two browsers exchange audio, video and data directly. The catch is that WebRTC gives you building blocks, not a finished feature. This guide walks through those blocks in the order you actually need them, with the exact API calls you need, and then covers the production issues that tutorials usually skip.

A browser-to-browser call has four moving parts:

Start with the local preview. Browsers only allow camera access on HTTPS or localhost, so serve your page accordingly.

1.     Request a stream with navigator.mediaDevices.getUserMedia(), passing video constraints (an ideal width of 1280 and height of 720 is a sensible default) and audio constraints with echoCancellation and noiseSuppression enabled.

2.     Assign the returned MediaStream to the srcObject property of your local video element.

3.     Keep a reference to the stream, because you will add its tracks to the peer connection later.

Set the muted and playsinline attributes on the local video element. Without muted users hear themselves, and without playsinline iOS Safari opens the video full screen.

The peers need a way to find each other. A tiny Node.js server using the ws package is enough for development. Its whole job is to relay messages between the peers in a room:

1.     Create a WebSocket server (for example with the ws package) listening on its own port.

2.     Keep a map of room names to the set of sockets in each room.

3.     When a client sends a join message, store the room name on the socket and add it to that room's set.

4.     For every other message type, forward the raw message to the other sockets in the same room, and never echo it back to the sender.

5.     On disconnect, remove the socket from its room so stale peers do not receive messages.

In production you would add authentication, limit room size to two for one-to-one calls, and validate message types, but the shape stays the same.

Both sides create an RTCPeerConnection, add their local tracks and listen for the remote ones:

1.     Create a new RTCPeerConnection with an iceServers list that contains at least one STUN server.

2.     Loop over the local stream's tracks and call addTrack() for each one.

3.     In the ontrack handler, attach the first remote stream to your remote video element.

4.     In the onicecandidate handler, send every new candidate to the other peer through your signalling channel as a candidate message.

One peer creates an offer, the other answers, and both apply each other's descriptions. Candidates arrive asynchronously in the background.

1.     The caller runs createOffer(), applies it with setLocalDescription() and sends the description as an offer message.

2.     The callee applies the offer with setRemoteDescription(), runs createAnswer(), applies it locally and sends it back as an answer.

3.     The caller applies the answer with setRemoteDescription().

4.     Both sides pass every incoming candidate message to addIceCandidate().

If both peers might start a call at the same time, look up the "perfect negotiation" pattern on MDN. It assigns one side as polite and resolves offer collisions cleanly instead of leaving both peers stuck.

On a home network, STUN alone often works. On corporate Wi-Fi, mobile carriers and symmetric NATs it frequently does not, and the call silently fails to connect. A TURN server relays media when a direct path is impossible. The open-source coturn server is the usual choice.

In practice, your iceServers list should contain your own STUN URL plus a TURN URL with a username and credential, so the browser can fall back to the relay automatically when direct connectivity fails.

Generate short-lived TURN credentials on your backend rather than hard-coding them, and budget for bandwidth: relayed calls pass every frame through your server.

Users deny camera access, unplug headsets and switch from Wi-Fi to 4G mid-call. Catch NotAllowedError and show a clear explanation, listen for devicechange events, and use RTCRtpSender.replaceTrack() to swap cameras without renegotiating the whole call.

Listen to pc.onconnectionstatechange. When the state becomes disconnected, wait a few seconds before giving up, because it often recovers. On failed, call pc.restartIce() to try new network paths.

Use RTCRtpSender.setParameters() to cap the bitrate on weak connections, and read pc.getStats() to monitor packet loss and round-trip time. Showing a small "poor connection" indicator does more for perceived quality than any codec tweak.

Mesh calls, where every participant connects to every other, work for two or three people. Beyond that, upload bandwidth explodes. Group calls need a Selective Forwarding Unit (SFU) such as mediasoup, LiveKit or Janus, which receives each stream once and forwards it to the others.

Tutorials end at a working demo, but the fastest way to understand what production WebRTC looks like is to watch a real call from the inside. Chrome ships an internal diagnostics page that shows every peer connection the browser opens, and it works on any site that uses WebRTC.

1.     Open chrome://webrtc-internals in one tab and keep it open.

2.     In another tab, start a call on your own demo and find its RTCPeerConnection entry.

3.     Expand that entry and look at the ICE candidate pairs: you will see whether the call went direct (host or srflx) or through a TURN relay (relay).

4.     Open the stats graphs for the outbound video stream and watch the bitrate, frame rate and resolution adapt when you throttle the network in DevTools.

5.     Check the negotiated codec and how quickly the connection recovers when you switch Wi-Fi off and back on.

Once you can read your own call, repeat the exercise on a production service. Any browser-based product works, whether a meeting tool or a live video chat that pairs two visitors, because webrtc-internals shows the same data for every site. Expect differences from your demo: more candidate pairs, a relay candidate in the list and a bitrate that adapts faster. Seeing them makes the earlier sections concrete, from why TURN matters to how bandwidth estimation reacts to packet loss.

The one-to-one call above is the core of many products, from telehealth consultations and tutoring to customer support. The engineering challenges grow with the use case: random matching needs queueing and presence on the signalling server, public platforms need moderation and reporting, and global audiences need TURN servers in several regions.

Start with the minimal version, get it working across Chrome, Firefox and Safari on both desktop and mobile, and add TURN before real users arrive. Once the call is reliable, every other feature becomes a much easier problem.

#10089. Shipping a Trillion Parameters With a Hub Bucket: Delta Weight Sync in TRL

TL;DR, because you have models to train and we respect that:

Async RL just got a lot cheaper. Read on.

If you read our previous post on the landscape of async RL training, you already know the punchline. Every async RL library, regardless of how it spells "actor model" or which color its NCCL backend is painted, eventually trips over the same root: weight synchronization.

The inference engine speaks the policy of step N. The trainer just finished step N+1. The fresh weights have to get from one side to the other before the inference engine starts drifting hopelessly off-policy. This sits on the critical path whether you are running sync or async: a blocking transfer is wasted idle compute of GPUs not generating tokens. With a sparse delta path you collapse that idle time into seconds, and the trainer does not even have to wait for the inference engine to be ready: it just publishes "weights ready" and uploads the weights to the shared bucket the moment its optimizer step finishes, while the inference engine fetches on its own time.

Fireworks put a very memorable number on this in their post Frontier RL Is Cheaper Than You Think: for a frontier 1T-parameter checkpoint at fp8 (their setting), a full snapshot is 1024 GiB, and that is what conventional wisdom says you have to ship every time you update your rollout fleet. That is the kind of number that gets people to start drawing diagrams with mega-clusters, RDMA fabrics, and dedicated cross-region links. Their measured average delta between adjacent checkpoints lands at 20.3 GiB, or 1.98% of the full model, and "more than 98% of weights in bf16 format remain bit-equivalent between consecutive checkpoints".

Cursor's Composer 2 report tells a parallel story. They run training and inference in different regions and stitch them together with a shared S3 bucket (their exact words), into which the trainer uploads compressed weight diffs every training step. Each cluster independently downloads and reconstructs from the shared delta chain, "requiring no direct connectivity to the training cluster". The two sides never speak to each other about parameters directly. The bucket is the wire.

Both papers agree on three things, and we want to repeat them slowly, because the rest of this post is essentially a faithful open source translation:

The only thing missing was a version of this story that you can pip install. So we wrote one.

Before we wire anything up, it is worth understanding why this whole game is even winnable. The "98% of weights do not change" claim sounds suspiciously like one of those numbers that works in the demo and falls apart in the wild. It is not. It falls out of how bf16 arithmetic works at the learning rates RL uses.

A bf16 number has 7 mantissa bits. Between two consecutive powers of two, there are exactly 27=1282^7 = 12827=128 representable values, so the spacing between adjacent bf16 numbers around ∣w∣|w|∣w∣ is roughly ∣w∣⋅2−7|w| \cdot 2^{-7}∣w∣⋅2−7. An update gets absorbed by the bf16 cast whenever it sits below half of that spacing, i.e., when ∣Δw∣<∣w∣/256|\Delta w| < |w|/256∣Δw∣<∣w∣/256. This is the "bf16 visibility threshold" PULSE plots in their Figure 3.

Now look at what Adam does. At an RL learning rate of, say, 3×10−63 \times 10^{-6}3×10−6, the update to a single weight is: Δw=−η⋅m^v^+ϵ\Delta w = -\eta \cdot \frac{\hat{m}}{\sqrt{\hat{v}} + \epsilon}Δw=−η⋅v^​+ϵm^​

The normalized step m^/(v^+ϵ)\hat{m}/(\sqrt{\hat{v}}+\epsilon)m^/(v^​+ϵ) is roughly order one, so ∣Δw∣≈η≈3×10−6|\Delta w| \approx \eta \approx 3 \times 10^{-6}∣Δw∣≈η≈3×10−6. For most weights, ∣w∣|w|∣w∣ sits somewhere around 10−210^{-2}10−2 to 10−110^{-1}10−1 (PULSE reports a median of 0.019 for representative LLM weights). The threshold ∣w∣/256|w|/256∣w∣/256 at that magnitude is around 4×10−54 \times 10^{-5}4×10−5 to 4×10−44 \times 10^{-4}4×10−4, which is bigger than the update.

In other words: the optimizer is whispering, and bf16 cannot hear it. The update gets absorbed by rounding, the byte representation of www does not change, and from the inference engine's perspective, this weight did not move. Multiply that by a few hundred million parameters, and you get the >99% sparsity number, for free, with zero approximation.

This is exactly the argument made formal in the PULSE paper (Mihai & Belilovsky, 2026). They define two thresholds. The absorption bound 10η10\eta10η is the conservative worst case for an Adam update, and the effective bound η\etaη is the regime you actually live in. The bf16 visibility threshold is ∣w∣/256|w|/256∣w∣/256. Whenever the update sits below the visibility threshold, it gets absorbed, and the bf16 byte does not change. Their Figure 3 plots both bounds against a cloud of representative LLM weights, and the conclusion is unambiguous: at η=3×10−6\eta = 3 \times 10^{-6}η=3×10−6, the absorption bound itself already sits below the visibility threshold for almost every weight in the model. They measure this empirically across Qwen2.5 (0.5B/1.5B/7B), Llama-3.2-3B, and Gemma-3-4B, and consistently find a mean per-step sparsity of ~99%, with a standard deviation of 0.2 to 0.4% over 400 training steps. The worst-case step stays above 98%. So <1% changed is not a lucky measurement; it is what the arithmetic guarantees.

We do not have to predict this analytically (and indeed, we tried predicting the change mask from Adam's mmm and vvv statistics, but recall was a sad 30%, more on that later). We just need to observe which bytes flipped. That is a tiny boolean tensor per parameter, computed right around the optimizer step.

Here is where the second piece of the story comes in, and where this post stops being a translation of Fireworks/Cursor and starts being a Hugging Face thing.

A Bucket is a repo type on the Hub designed for high-frequency object storage. No commit ceremony, no PR workflow, no LFS quirks. You add files, you list files, you download files. The Python interface is two functions:

That is it. Two function calls and your weights are in flight.

Under the hood, buckets are backed by Xet, the Hub's content-defined chunking storage layer. Xet looks at every file you upload, slices it into chunks based on its actual content (not fixed offsets), and deduplicates against everything already in the bucket. The practical upshot, which is delightful in this context, is that even if we were too lazy to write the sparse encoding and just uploaded full anchors every step, Xet would still only transfer the changed chunks. Sparse encoding + Xet stack: we pay for what moved, and we pay for it once.

This is the open source equivalent of the "shared S3 bucket" both Fireworks and Cursor reach for, except the storage layer already knows about content hashing, your existing HF token already has permission, and it composes natively with the rest of the stack (Spaces, datasets, models).

The full architecture has exactly three boxes and one shared substrate:

The property to internalize, the one Cursor's paper sells hard and that holds verbatim here: the trainer and the rollout server never talk to each other about weights. They exchange a tiny POST containing {"repo_id": ..., "filename": ...}, and that is the entire control plane. The actual byte transfer happens between each side and the bucket, in parallel, with no shared network fabric.

The trainer writes. Replicas read. The Hub does the plumbing.

Now we can open the hood. The protocol has four parts: a wire format, a bucket layout, a 30 line vLLM extension, and a trainer side change detector. It is honestly less code than it sounds.

We picked safetensors for the on-disk and on-wire format. It is already the canonical checkpoint format on the Hub, every reasonable framework can read it, and the header carries arbitrary string metadata. That metadata field is where we hide the protocol.

There are two kinds of files in the bucket.

Anchors look like a normal checkpoint: one tensor per parameter, full bf16 weights, written every NNN syncs (we default to N=10N=10N=10).

Deltas are the interesting bit. For each parameter that actually changed, we store two entries: a flat int32 tensor of element indices, and a bf16 tensor of values at those indices.

The cadence is straightforward: anchor every Nth step, delta in between. Both end up in the same bucket under anchors/ and deltas/ prefixes. Each new inference replica only needs to grab the most recent anchor and then replay the deltas since.

The trainer needs to know which bf16 elements actually flipped. We do this with a tiny BF16ChangeDetector that registers a pre-step and post-step hook on the optimizer:

The actual code in the PR has a bit more plumbing (matching optimizer param objects to model params via data_ptr(), because Accelerate wraps them as different Python objects), but the idea fits on a napkin: snapshot, step, diff.

This is ground truth. We tried the more elegant path of predicting the mask from Adam's mmm and vvv statistics, using the bf16 ULP threshold directly. It works in principle. In practice, recall was around 30%, which means we would have shipped a delta missing two thirds of the actual updates. Adam's normalization is messy enough that the analytical threshold is not tight. So we just compare bytes. It costs one bf16 CPU snapshot of the model on the trainer side, which we are willing to pay.

The four phases of the new _sync_weight flow are:

The line that matters is the parenthesis. Inference was paused for 1.1 seconds. The remaining 9.4 seconds were spent uploading, which occurred while the rollout server was still generating tokens. With NCCL, we were paying the full sync time as pause time. Here we are paying for it as background time.

vLLM has a clean abstraction for this called WeightTransferEngine. We implement a DeltaWeightTransferEngine whose receive_weights method is, in spirit:

We register it via vLLM's --worker-extension-cls flag, which means no fork of vLLM is required. You install TRL into the same image as vLLM, point the CLI at our class, and you are done.

Worth mentioning: vLLM itself has an in-flight effort to land sparse weight transfer natively, vllm-project/vllm#40096. It adds receive_sparse_weights() and trainer_send_sparse_weights() directly on the WeightTransferEngine base class, with patches encoded as (indices, values) and applied in place via index_copy_(), removing the GPU/CPU validation roundtrip entirely. The PR reports a transfer of 0.16 MB in 0.40 ms for a sparse patch on Qwen3-1.7B versus 942 MB in 192 ms for a full dense send.

One honest caveat in our implementation on the inference side: we keep a CPU bf16 snapshot of the model so we can reconstruct full tensors from sparse (indices, values) patches, because load_weights in vLLM today expects full tensors. Once #40096 (or its successor) lands and exposes an in-place sparse load_weights path, we can apply the indices directly on the GPU and drop the snapshot!

This is the part we are smug about. Everything we have described so far works on your laptop, but the point of routing weights through a Hub bucket is that the trainer and the rollout server do not have to live anywhere near each other. So we ran a fully disaggregated training with three machines, none of which share a network:

Setting this up is genuinely a few hf CLI calls. The vLLM Space's Dockerfile is essentially the upstream vLLM image plus pip install trl@... plus the entrypoint:

And kick off training from anywhere on the planet that can talk HTTPS:

The trainer never opens a port. The Space never sees the trainer's IP. The Wordle environment does not know either of them exists. They all talk to the Hub. Training converged on the immediate-EOS sanity check, then on real Wordle rollouts: reward went up, delta payloads stayed in the 20 to 35 MB band, and the inference-paused window per sync stayed around a second. The full run logs are linked in the companion PR.

Async RL training without a cluster. If you have one GPU and a Hugging Face account, you can now do real disaggregated training. Your trainer is on the GPU; your rollout fleet lives in Spaces; your environment lives in another Space; weights move through a bucket. This used to require either a colocated setup (with all the throughput compromises that brings) or a real cluster with shared networking. It does not anymore.

Multi-replica inference, for free. Stand up two vLLM Spaces, or ten. They all pull from the same bucket. Xet content-addresses storage so consecutive anchors share chunks at rest (which keeps your bucket from blowing up), and the Hub's edge cache makes repeated downloads of the same file cheap to serve. Want a globally distributed rollout fleet? That is now a small DevOps exercise, not a research project.

A wire format you can debug with your existing tools. A delta is a safetensors file. You can safe_open it from a notebook, list its keys, inspect the indices, compute the sparsity yourself. We have spent enough hours in tcpdump on opaque NCCL streams to appreciate this.

A path to frontier scale. The 20 to 35 MB number is for Qwen3-0.6B. The interesting question is what the curve looks like once you turn the dial up. Let us do the napkin math.

Take Llama-3.1-405B. In bf16 that is 810 GB on disk. PULSE measures ~99% mean per-step sparsity at RL learning rates, so the actual delta sits around 1% of the parameters. Their deployment-measured encoding hits 108 MB on a 7B model, which is the ~130× reduction PULSE reports. Scaled linearly to 405B, the delta lands at roughly 6 GB per step.

What does that buy you in wall-clock? NCCL is fast inside a cluster, sure. Assume a generous 100 GB/s aggregate broadcast bandwidth (multi-node, RDMA, the works). A full sync is 810 GB / 100 GB/s ≈ 8 seconds of inference pause, every step. With the delta path, the trainer streams 6 GB to a bucket in the background while generation keeps running, and the rollout server's actual paused window is just the apply step, which on this scale lands at a couple of seconds. So even before we leave the cluster, delta cuts the visible pause by 4× and the bytes on the wire by ~130×.

Now leave the cluster. NCCL straight up does not work across clouds. Once you want a rollout fleet in us-east, another in eu-west, maybe one in a Hugging Face Space, the bucket-based path is the only path. At 1 GB/s of usable internet bandwidth, a single full broadcast would take 13 minutes; the delta does it in 6 seconds.

For a 1 TB-class model in the Fireworks framing, their own measured numbers show 20.3 GiB deltas vs the 1024 GiB full snapshot, a ~50× reduction. PULSE's tighter, sparse encoding would push that further (extrapolating ~15 GB per delta, closer to ~65×). Either way, you are in a regime where shipping weights through commodity object storage stops being a hack and starts being the only sensible architecture.

#10086. Reachy Mini goes fully local

After building your Reachy Mini, you'll install the conversation app and start talking to it. Until now, you had to send your audio to a server. But not anymore. Today we'll walk you through running the whole stack locally.

This stack is powered by speech-to-speech, our cascaded VAD → STT → LLM → TTS pipeline that exposes a Realtime API-compatible /v1/realtime WebSocket. Once you launch the backend, point the robot at it from the UI.

Cascades are the most flexible option in the open-source landscape today, and with the right pieces they're also the fastest. We'll recommend the components we like best, but the whole point of a cascade is that you can swap them. New models drop every week.

This blog walks you through running conversations with Reachy Mini fully locally. No cloud, no API keys, no data leaving your machine. Here's a video showing this live:

To serve the LLM, we'll use Hugging Face's llama.cpp. If you need to install it, the simplest way is brew install llama.cpp or winget install llama.cpp, for more help, check the docs. First, we'll run:

And done! The first time it will download the model, subsequent launches are fast.

We'll begin by simply installing the library

Then, while we are serving the LLM in another terminal, we can simply run:

And you can start talking to the model through your terminal! The first time it will need to download Parakeet-TDT 0.6B v3 and Qwen3TTS, but subsequent launches are fast.

Here's a video showing the local conversation mode:

Now, after you've tried it in --mode local, you can run again the command without that option to serve speech-to-speech to the robot.

Once you have llama.cpp and speech-to-speech running, you can start the robot with the desktop app and launch the conversation app. In the UI from the conversation app, you need to choose the local mode by clicking on "edit connection" in the HF backend. Here's a video showing how to do it:

And you're done. You can start talking to your robot. Every stage of the pipeline is a trade-off: there are faster TTS models with lower quality, slower STT models with higher quality. We optimized for multilingual, you might want to optimize for a single language. The rest of the blog covers how to customize.

Hosted realtime backends are convenient, but running your own engine unlocks three things:

The speech-to-speech repo gives you all of that in a single CLI. It boots a WebSocket server at /v1/realtime that speaks the same protocol Reachy Mini already knows how to talk to.

A cascaded voice pipeline has four stages: VAD, STT, LLM, and TTS. For three of them, we pick solid defaults so you can focus on the LLM:

We are opinionated about these choices, feel free to swap them out for your own if you have a preference.

The LLM is the layer with the most impact on latency and overall performance of the system. We support two options: run a model locally (llama.cpp, MLX, Transformers, vLLM), or use a server with a Responses API (OpenAI, Gemini, HF Inference Endpoints, llama.cpp, vLLM, etc).

The main bottleneck in the system is LLM inference latency. To address that, we support external inference engines exposed through the Responses API protocol.

The speech-to-speech engine therefore supports a second mode where the LLM lives in a separate process as long as it speaks the Responses API protocol. You launch your model server in one terminal, you launch the voice loop in another terminal, and the two talk over HTTP.

Requires vLLM ≥ 0.21.0. Full support for the Responses API protocol, including tool-call streaming used by the speech-to-speech backend, landed in vLLM 0.21.0. Older versions will boot but trip up as soon as the assistant tries to call a tool.

When serving a model through vLLM for this pipeline, three flags are effectively required:

Terminal 1: vLLM inference server (Qwen/Qwen3-4B-Instruct-2507):

The --speculative-config line enables Multi-Token Prediction (MTP). It is optional, but it has a great impact on end-to-end latency. Leave it on whenever the model supports it.

Same protocol, but the model runs on a managed GPU on Hugging Face. Deploy any chat model as an Inference Endpoint, then point the voice loop at the endpoint URL:

If you don't want to manage your own endpoint, use an Inference Provider. Hugging Face routes your request to a third-party backend (e.g. Together, Fireworks, Replicate) with a single URL:

When you want to test against a frontier model with zero infra, point the same flag at OpenAI:

The --responses_api_* flags work the same for any provider that implements the protocol (OpenRouter, Together, Fireworks, …). Swap the base URL and the API key, keep the rest of the pipeline identical.

If you are on a Mac, MLX is the lowest-friction way to run a real model with sane latency. We recommend Qwen3-4B-Instruct-2507, which is small enough to feel instant on M-series chips and capable enough to hold a conversation.

The server listens on ws://127.0.0.1:8765/v1/realtime by default. Leave it running, connect the conversation app to the local backend, and you are talking to your robot.

Same idea, but using vanilla transformers. Use this if you are on a CUDA box, on Linux, or if you want to swap models freely without re-converting weights for MLX.

Tip. Qwen3-4B-Instruct-2507 is another good option for LLM because it gives a good speed/quality balance on a single consumer GPU. You can point --model_name at any HF model the backend supports — for example a larger Gemma, Qwen, or a Mistral.

If you are running the voice engine on your laptop and the conversation app on a Reachy Mini Wireless, the only thing that changes is the URL. Make sure the engine binds to a LAN address (not just 127.0.0.1) and use the laptop's IP from the robot when you select the IP in the UI.

If you don't know your IP, here's how to find it:

Look for "IPv4 Address" under your active adapter.

You want the 192.168.x.x or 10.x.x.x one. If you see 169.254.x.x, you're not actually on the network.

Star huggingface/speech-to-speech and pollen-robotics/reachy_mini_conversation_app, and come tell us in the discussions which open-source cascade you ended up running on your robot.

#10084. PwC's CISO on AI, Robots & What's Next for Security

As AI accelerates change across the enterprise, PwC's James Shira explains why security teams must rethink their approach to risk and adapt their strategies.

James Shira, global CISO and CIO of PwC, has spent more than two decades navigating the evolution of cybersecurity, from its early days as a largely technical function to its continuously growing role in corporate agendas and spending. Shira's path into the industry was, as he puts it, as "consistent and inconsistent as the paths people follow." Originally considering a career in law, Shira decided to pivot, more seriously considering pursuing cybersecurity through independent study, and then formal education. Today, he oversees both technology and security at one of the world's largest professional services firms, giving him a broad perspective on the challenges facing security leaders.

In this episode of Heard It From a CISO with Dark Reading associate editor Kristina Beek, Shira discusses the skills and experience needed to build a career in cybersecurity, including the value of industry certifications, higher education, and on-the-job experience. He also examines the qualities that distinguish effective security teams, the challenges of balancing the CISO and CIO roles, and how security leaders can establish credibility with corporate boards. For Shira, successful leadership comes down to more than technical expertise. It involves building trust, communicating complex issues clearly, and creating an environment where employees can develop.

Related:As Test Takers Turn to AI, Exam Security Plays Catch-Up

Shira also shares his thoughts on the topic on everyone's minds: artificial intelligence. He warns that rapid adoption is expanding attack surfaces, adding pressure on security teams, but also notes that AI technology will add opportunities for professionals seeking roles in the field. As for what's ahead, Shira expects significant societal and industry change and shares that this rate of change is likely to be the new standard — it’s best if everyone is prepared to go along for the ride.

This is part of Dark Reading's ongoing Heard It From a CISO video series, which features frank, exclusive conversations with cybersecurity leaders in the trenches. Check out the entire series here.

This transcript has been edited for clarity and length by Informa TechTarget's internal AI assistant. For the full experience, please watch the video.

James Shira: I think there's a lot of strength in diversity of experience and perspective, and so we try to embrace that. I like people who are self-confident and have their own point of view. It makes for mutual learning and some intense debates at times. But I think that makes for better decisions.

Related:Attackers in Binance Breach Targeted Known Weakness, Missing Controls

Dark Reading's Kristina Beek: Hi, everyone. My name is Kristina Beek. I'm an associate editor at Dark Reading, and I'm here for another episode of Heard It From a CISO. Today, I'm joined by James Shira. Thank you so much for joining us. I would love it if you could introduce yourself and talk about your background and your current role as CISO at PwC.

James Shira: Sure. It's great to be with you today. My name is James. I am the global CISO and CIO for PwC. I've been involved in what we used to call IT security since 1999. I became a CISO in the early 2000s, I think 2000 or 2001, really based on an opportunity and happenstance. I've been involved in the community since that time, now 25 or 26 years. For the last eight years, I've also been operating as our global CIO.

DR's Kristina Beek: Love to hear that. How did you first get involved specifically in cybersecurity, technology, or security in general? I know there are a lot of different ways people get involved. Some people study computer science, and some come from very alternative backgrounds. What does your path look like?

James Shira: I think my path is probably as consistent and inconsistent as the paths people follow. I was planning on getting a degree to become a lawyer, actually. Then, being a blue-collar kid, I realized I couldn't afford law school. After two years, I needed to make a change, so I redirected toward business and information systems. That was my undergraduate background.

Related:Getting Past the Post-Quantum Cryptography Discovery Phase

When I graduated in 1998, there was a bit of a mini-recession, what we often refer to as the dot-com crash. At the time, I used to read the physical Wall Street Journal pretty religiously, and there was a lot of discussion about security. We didn't call it cyber then. I figured this was a space that needed leaders and leadership. I was very interested in working toward and building an executive career path, and I wasn't sure — probably like a lot of college graduates — how to go from having no experience to having an opportunity to be in a role like the ones I'm privileged to have today.

I really started by researching, reading, learning, and studying, a lot of self-directed study, including some computer science-based material. I also did a program at Columbia that's now a master's program, which was very helpful to me. I was one of the first students when we started. The idea was like an MBA for technologists, and I'm proud to say it's now a Master of Science degree. I had the opportunity to be a student mentor there for a long time. It was really on a whim that I thought this space was going to be incredibly interesting, and it's proven to be.

DR's Kristina Beek: That brings me to my next question: What would you recommend to somebody who wants to go into cybersecurity today? In general, what would your advice be? What insights could you provide in terms of what would be best to study? Should they prioritize certifications or a four-year education? There are a lot of different ways to go into cybersecurity today.

James Shira: For sure. I think the four-year education discussion we're all having right now is really relevant. I have younger kids, so I've got some time before they get there. I think it's a really relevant conversation because of the cost. Having worked my way through college and taken out loans at the time, those loan amounts look really small compared with what people are confronted with today. I think it's a very fair question and debate that people should have.

I'm a big proponent of certification on our security team. We really encourage people to do it, and we sponsor some of them. I'm not going to name them because we'd be here for a long time, but I think it's a very smart strategy.

The way I describe it to our folks is that I talk about the concepts of internal equity and external equity. Your internal equity when you come out of college is zero. You're new; you're coming into the industry. You build that up over time with your employer. Obviously, you want to pick the right place to work, as best you can. In the early days, experience in and of itself is the value you're pursuing.

The second piece, external equity, is something you can drive as hard as you want. As a young person without a lot of experience, you can pursue certifications. Some require years of work, but there's a lot out there. The most successful people I've had the privilege to mentor start out with a high degree of emphasis on certifications. Then, after five to seven years of experience, they make a choice about whether they're going to pursue a management track or a higher-end technical director or subject-matter-expert track.

On your question about a four-year education versus certifications, my personal view is that if you want to be in a role similar to mine, or the same as mine, you're going to want that four-year degree. You may even want a master's eventually. If that's your intended path, I would encourage you, notwithstanding the loans, to complete your undergraduate degree. There are a lot of great schools with programs that can be helpful. If you look at that and say to yourself, "That's a significant debt burden, and I don't think it makes sense. I'm not sure I want to pursue being an executive," then I think you should do the certifications and work on getting as much experience as you can.

DR's Kristina Beek: That's a great insight. You talked about building equity and how, when you're fresh out of college, that really depends on your employer and the company you choose to work for. Moving back to PwC, what interested you in the company? Why did you choose to work there, and what has it been like being CISO?

James Shira: When I was coming out of Zurich Financial Services, now Zurich Insurance Group — which was also a great time in my career — I was interested in finding the right CISO challenge at a similar or bigger scale. What interested me about PwC at that time was that it was a 160-plus-year-old institution. I had never worked in professional services; I had only worked in financial services. So a different industry interested me.

I think the organization's values here at PwC were very consistent with mine, and it's been a privilege to be here. It sounds clichéd, but it's really a great place. The quality of people, on average, in my experience, has been really high. People have a desire to do the right thing, and as a CISO, that's incredibly helpful. A lot of our security strategy is culturally centered on employee behavior and training, so those things were very consistent and have been very helpful.

I know some CISOs drive programs through cultures that are less amenable. This culture was incredibly amenable to moving its security program to the next level. Nobody's program is perfect, but that was helpful. Lastly, I had the opportunity to bring a lot of my colleagues with me. I have the privilege of sitting in these roles, but it's not something I did on my own. It's something we've done collectively as a team. Given the scale of the mission here, I had the opportunity to bring some colleagues from my previous employer over, and it's been awesome to see their careers flourish here as well. In short, it's a great place to work.

DR's Kristina Beek: That brings me to a follow-up question. When it comes to a team, whether it's business-oriented or security-focused, what makes a great team? What kinds of people are you looking for, whether in terms of personality or skills?

James Shira: I'm going to answer your question in reverse order. The people I like to work with don't come in a common package. I think there's a lot of strength in diversity of experience and perspective, and so we try to embrace that. I like people who are self-confident and have their own point of view. It makes for mutual learning and some intense debates at times, but I think that makes for better decisions.

The people I'm looking for don't have to have gone to a specific school. They don't necessarily need a traditional profile, but they definitely need to be self-confident and self-directed. I talk to the team a lot about emotional resiliency. I think it's a really important concept in the security industry because, when I got started, security was past the mailroom, past the bathrooms, in the basement somewhere, and rarely in the boardroom. Now, people coming into the field wouldn't even recognize that, because security is such a central, strategically critical issue for companies. I need that confidence in our employees so that, when they become the leaders they can be, they can flourish based on that confidence. It's hard to build a great team without that.

The second piece I think is incredibly important is transparency. It's something I work diligently to practice when I'm speaking in front of the thousands of colleagues I have the privilege of leading: being as brutally transparent as possible about whatever we're trying to do. It's uncomfortable at times, and it can be challenging to answer the questions you get, but I think it provokes the kind of cultural engagement that makes for a great team.

The one thing I'll say lastly is that I don't think mediocrity, as a rule, fits in high-performing teams. You have to embrace your high performers, try to elevate and promote them, and create an environment where they can be as self-directed and successful as they can be.

DR's Kristina Beek: Absolutely. When you were answering that, one of the things you talked about was how the CISO role and cybersecurity in general are now in the boardroom. I see a lot of articles about how to communicate with C-suite members as a CISO, how to deal with friction, and how to get your board to believe you. What would you say about communicating your needs as a CISO to the rest of the board? Do you encounter friction in your experience, and how do you deal with that?

James Shira: I think it's a great question. I'm going to offer a point of view. I'll start by saying I've gotten it wrong. I don't have all the answers, but I've learned through mistakes and by having great mentors.

I think credibility with a board starts, frankly, through delivery. The first thing you have to do is build a track record as best you can. That might sound counterintuitive: Don't I need the board's buy-in before I deliver? Somewhat, but I think conversations with our various boards here, and the conversations I've had previously, show that over time, through delivery of the program and driving the change you're advocating for, you can build a lot of credibility.

The second of my three points is that you have to find your own authentic voice. Personally, I'm not a natural. I kind of joke with the team at times that I'm a radio guy, not a TV guy, and I've had to work at being a TV guy. You have to find your own authenticity through your own style. A lot of times, those of us who get the privilege of being in these C-level jobs receive a lot of advice and pressure about how to present and who to be. I would encourage people listening to find their own style and approach that works best for them. Obviously, measure it against how effective it is, but embrace the style that's authentic to you. For me, I just try to be myself with our board.

The last thing I'd say, and I think it's maybe the most important point, is that you have to bring the expertise to the board, not try to drag the board to your expertise. In our domain, don't underestimate how intimidating it can be for the people listening. It's security. They see the headlines. Maybe an issue has occurred in that business. As board members, they feel responsible for providing oversight over management, and they're under tremendous pressure to do so. Don't underestimate that.

If you come at them with a high degree of expertise, terms, acronyms, and things they don't understand, I've found that doesn't work. That would be one of the mistakes I've made in the past. What's worked well for me is not to dumb it down, but to simplify it. If you have enough mastery of a topic, you can describe it in a way that doesn't make the other person feel intimidated and helps them say, "OK, I get that." One suggestion I would offer is to use storytelling. That's what I've done, and it has worked well for me.

DR's Kristina Beek: While you're obviously CISO, you're also CIO, so you have two perspectives. What is it like balancing the responsibilities of both roles?

James Shira: The good news is that, over the last eight years I've had the privilege of being in these roles, there's been a tremendous amount of harmonization between the technology transformation of large enterprises and the need to get the cyber piece right. Therefore, unlike when I started, when security was past the mailroom and in the basement, it's now such a primary issue for organizations that it's really on the CIO's agenda. I think having both of those skill sets is a very critical thing in this day and age.

The one difference I'd acknowledge for the audience, because otherwise anybody watching would think I missed it, is that at times the CIO role can be inherently more political than the CISO role. Let me explain briefly. As a CISO, you objectively know what good looks like: Don't have a breach, don't have an incident, improve your audit posture, drive good risk management, and so on. What good looks like in the CIO world can sometimes be less black and white and more gray. It can change in a way that a traditional CISO might find challenging to navigate.

I, for one, never anticipated the amount of passion and energy that debating different HR or finance platforms might bring. I've learned how to spend a lot of time with CFOs and COOs in our businesses. That's made me not only better professionally, but also more sympathetic to the issues they have, especially in some of the smaller businesses where a decision we might make from a CIO perspective has a significant material impact on their cost basis. There are differences, but in summary, it's a very complementary experience for me. The biggest challenge is time management and moving time between the different things.

DR's Kristina Beek: Absolutely. AI is, of course, always part of the conversation. It's changing how attackers work, and it's also changing how organizations operate. What do you see as the biggest cybersecurity opportunity or risk associated with AI right now?

James Shira: I think the most important issue with AI, straight down the middle, is how it changes, evolves, and increases an organization's attack surface. The second issue is the rate of change it brings: how fast it moves and how fast systems have to move. Those are the two dynamics.

What happens to the size of your attack surface? AI can really explode it. At the same time, AI puts pressure on the pace of change across the whole security function. For us specifically, that means dealing with the amount of patching, vulnerability management, inbound requests, and client requests. You have to manage those two dynamics.

On the technology front, in my career — which some people in this audience might think is long, while others might think it's not that long yet — I've never seen anything move as fast. In a short period of time, we've gone from a nascent technology that we're all excited about to actually operationalizing it. At least in my career, I haven't seen anything cross that divide so quickly. Therefore, I think it's ultimately the biggest change-management exercise, maybe ever. That's really where leaders need to center and focus their time.

DR's Kristina Beek: A lot of people are coming out of college or going into college with the expectation of going into cybersecurity or computer science. AI is changing the field very rapidly. A lot of people are scared that they may not even have a job or that there may not be a place for them in this field. What would you say to that, with the rise of AI?

James Shira: I understand where people get that. I understand how people get that. I think it's understandable, but I think it's wrong. The amount of change across society and industries is significant. It's very difficult for me to chart a course in my head for what isn't going to change. Therefore, I think the opportunity for young professionals is to be the change agents — to deliver the change.

I think one thing we don't always do well for our young professionals, but need to, is tell them the truth about the adversity of change management. It's hard. It's hard, and it's going to be hard for them. Do I think AI is a job-elimination technology? I don't. But I understand and respect how people might reach that conclusion.

If you're doing highly repetitive, data-centric activities, that's not, frankly, what you go to college for. Some of us had to do that coming out of college, earning our stripes, but that's not generally what you go to college for. That probably gets changed a lot by AI. Of course. I don't think it's a displacement strategy.

DR's Kristina Beek: Going back to what you said about how AI is changing things so rapidly, what do you think cybersecurity leaders will spend the most time thinking about three to five years from now? I know that's hard because things are changing so quickly, but what do you see for the future?

James Shira: I think the constants I would expect not to go away are the rate of change, the pace, and the pressure. Therefore, I think you have to find consistency in process and strategic principles, meaning how you manage your strategy shouldn't change. You should find the things in executing the strategy and operationalizing it that don't need to change, because so much around you will be changing.

In our history, and in at least my part of the 20-year history of IT security and cybersecurity, when there's been a technical change — think cloud, client-server, mobile, or whatever — we've effectively changed every aspect of how we implemented security controls. I'm hoping and working diligently to avoid repeating that pattern in the AI space because I think it just adds too much volume to an already high-intensity, high-volume situation.

Three to five years from now, I'm hoping AI can be a much more consistent enabler of delivering secure outcomes, but we're still learning how to fully operationalize it. Then there's the issue of token costs, which we're not going to get into today, but that has a high degree of relationship to driving the overall security budget, which we're figuring out as we go.

Secondly, I don't think most companies will have enough money to build a security program the way we've historically done it, at the size and scale that AI could imply would be required. Third, I think organizations are going to have to shrink their digital footprint as they transform. The good news is that — obviously, hope is not a strategy — AI will hopefully allow us to interact with our systems of state much more efficiently than building applications as the recurring front door to all of our systems, as we've done for the last 10 or 20 years. That ought to have a great benefit in reducing the attack surface, too. I think that's what companies need to do, and I think that's what will look so different in three to five years.

Lastly, I'd say I'm expecting significant societal and industry change, especially in a five-year window. I'm not sure I'm going to have a robot at home, but maybe some of us will. I think physical AI is going to place a significant premium on investment capacity, both on the hardware side and on the adoption and implementation side.

There are Orwellian views of that, where you could see the doom and gloom. I think there's also a tremendous opportunity. Some countries are not having the birth rates we need. Frankly, there isn't enough reproduction to maintain the number of people in society. So robots in some places in the world are going to be incredibly helpful in allowing us to deliver the things people need in society.

But I'm excited by it. I'll summarize by saying I think the big fundamental choice you have to make every morning when you wake up is to embrace the change, both in yourself and in how you do the job, because the change is almost — I joked with a colleague the other day, and she's a really capable runner while I am not, that this is kind of like being on the treadmill at the speed Annie would go at, not the speed James would go at. Some days I feel like I'm hanging in there, and other days I feel like I'm about to fall off the back of the treadmill. I think everybody just needs to say that's part of this.

DR's Kristina Beek: Absolutely. That's great to hear. Normally, I end these interviews by asking what the future of cybersecurity looks like to you, but we've already touched on that. So I'd rather end with a different question: You've spent a lot of time in tech and security and have seen how it's evolved. What has been the most rewarding part of that work, and what do you think will continue to challenge or motivate you, especially in a field where the risks are sometimes really high?

James Shira: Sure. It's an easy answer for me: It's the people part. It's the team. Every success I've had the privilege of being part of is not a James thing. I had a role, sure, but it's a team thing.

When you see someone — we have a number of people in our organization who started as interns at my previous employer. One colleague started as an intern and is now an executive. Another colleague, Annie, whom I mentioned, is now a partner. Those are the things that lift me back up when I have a bad day, which happens. It's when we see people building and shining in their own way, self-actualizing. That's pretty cool, and I think that's the right way things should work.

Look, it doesn't always work that way. There are probably people on the team who don't feel they got a fair chance, or who feel something didn't go perfectly. That's the challenge of working in teams of people, because people — me, you, all of us — are not perfect.

But the best days for me are when I see colleagues rise, shine, and do great things, and even leave the organization and go do great things somewhere else. That's pretty awesome. I think that's our opportunity with AI and security. We have to embrace it, try to see the positive in it, and grow through it.

DR's Kristina Beek: Absolutely. I so enjoyed this conversation. Thank you so much for joining me today.

James Shira: Me too. Thanks for your time.

Kristina Beek is associate editor at Dark Reading, where she covers a wide range of cybersecurity topics and spearheads video-related content, where she contributes both content and production skills to Dark Reading's expanding video coverage. She is the creator and host of the Heard It From a CISO video series, where she interviews CISOs, directors, and other industry strategists to provide insights into the ever-evolving cybersecurity landscape. In addition to her editorial work, Kristina manages Dark Reading's social media channels (including social video), and has held numerous roles within Dark Reading over the years, including copy editor and breaking news reporter, before transitioning her focus to multimedia journalism.

Kristina graduated from North Carolina State University in 2021 with a degree in Political Science, concentrating in law and justice, and a minor in English. During her time at NC State, she honed her writing skills by contributing opinion pieces to the university's newspaper, as well as writing fiction, poetry, and short essays. Upon graduating, she began her career as a content editor, focusing on higher education topics before joining Dark Reading in December of 2022.

Currently based in Washington D.C., you can find Kristina reading, taking walks in Georgetown, trying all the restaurants she can, and taking pictures of all the dogs she sees.

#10083. Hostinger VPS in 2026: Hands-On With the AI-Managed VPS

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

A few years ago, renting a VPS meant signing up to be a part-time sysadmin. You’d SSH into a blank Ubuntu prompt and lose a Saturday to Nginx configs and firewall rules before writing a single line of your actual project.

In 2026, three things have changed. What we build has changed: AI coding tools turn weekend ideas into working apps, and AI agents need a machine that stays on after your laptop closes. Who runs servers has changed: you can now ask an AI agent in your terminal to set up a reverse proxy, close a port or work out why something broke. And what servers cost has changed: the AI boom is soaking up the world’s memory supply, and hosting prices are rising with it.

So I bought the smallest Hostinger VPS plan, deployed a Node.js app in Docker, and handed the DevOps work to Hostinger Agent, the AI assistant built into the dashboard.

Below is what that felt like step by step and whether it’s worth locking in a price before they climb further.

Most VPS hosting for developers now falls into four buckets. They all run on the same kind of machine; what changes is how much RAM you give them.

Apps built with AI coding tools. Claude Code and Cursor get you to a working Node.js or Python app fast, then leave you wondering where to put it. A VPS gives you one fixed monthly bill instead of usage-based pricing. If you want push-to-deploy, Hostinger offers Ubuntu templates with Coolify or Dokploy preinstalled.

AI agents and automations that run 24/7. For most people, a “VPS for AI” means a CPU box that never sleeps, not a GPU. Think n8n workflows, a scheduled scraper, or your own agent in a Docker container. Hostinger even has an “Ubuntu 24.04 with Claude Code” template: SSH in, run claude /login, and the agent keeps working after you close your laptop.

APIs, backends and databases for side projects. A Postgres instance, a Redis cache and a small API behind a reverse proxy fit comfortably on a mid-sized plan. You pick the versions, the extensions and the backup schedule.

Client sites and stores. Freelancers outgrow shared hosting when one client needs a custom PHP extension or a WooCommerce store starts to crawl. A VPS with cPanel or Plesk, or a WordPress or WooCommerce template, keeps client work isolated and under your control.

If you’d rather not build anything from scratch, the Docker Manager catalog listed 1,017 one-click templates when I checked, including 93 under AI/ML and 162 under Developer tools.

For this Hostinger VPS review, the question I cared about was simple: how long from “Choose plan” to an app on the internet? On KVM 1, the entry plan, it was about 12 minutes. Here’s each step with rough timings.

I went with KVM 1: 1 vCPU, 4 GB RAM, 50 GB NVMe storage and 4 TB of bandwidth. On the Black Friday deal it costs $6.49/mo, paid upfront as $155.76 for 24 months, and renews at $11.99/mo.

You choose the server’s location and what to install during checkout, alongside your billing details. The location picker shows estimated latency for each data centre; mine showed about 80 ms.

Install options come in three tabs: Plain OS, Control panel and Applications. I picked plain Ubuntu 26.04 LTS to see how much work the AI would take off my hands. A daily backup add-on is offered, but weekly backups are already included.

The five-minute estimate was about right. The “you’re ready” screen then gives you two ways in: the VPS dashboard, or a pre-filled ssh root@ command. It also offers a free domain for a year to use as the server’s hostname.

The overview shows the OS, plan, CPU, RAM, disk and bandwidth at a glance, with Docker Manager, Backups & Monitoring, Security and DNS Manager in the side menu.

Every server also gets a hostname under hstgr.cloud (mine was srvXXXXXXX.hstgr.cloud), which came in handy later for SSL. I’ve masked my hostname as srvXXXXXXX throughout and blurred IP addresses in the screenshots.

Plain Ubuntu doesn’t ship with Docker. Open Docker Manager in hPanel and it installs Docker for you with one click. From there you can deploy apps from a Compose file, a repository URL or the one-click catalog.

Click Web console and you’re logged in as root in a browser tab, with Hostinger Agent in a panel beside it. You don’t need an SSH client or keys. The login banner flagged 33 pending updates, 23 of them security fixes; more on that later. A quick docker --version confirmed Docker 29.9.3 was ready.

Here’s the whole app: a tiny HTTP server with a health check, and a Dockerfile on Node.js 24, a supported LTS line.

The build took 8.3 seconds, including pulling node:24-alpine, and the health check answered straight away. The --restart unless-stopped flag brings the container back after a crash or reboot, which I tested later.

That’s a working app, but on plain HTTP, on a high port, with no TLS. Getting it production-ready is the DevOps part I handed to the AI.

An AI-managed VPS isn’t the same as a traditional managed VPS. You still get a self-managed server with full root access, but Hostinger Agent does the work you’d normally do yourself. Agent (previously called Kodee) is an MCP-powered assistant that lives in the dashboard and beside the AI web terminal, and it’s included at no extra cost. You can also connect Claude or Cursor to your server through Hostinger’s MCP server.

My prompt: “Check that Docker is installed, then set up a reverse proxy with a free SSL certificate so my demo-app container (port 3000) is served at https://srvXXXXXXX.hstgr.cloud.”

It started by looking around: the Docker and Compose versions, which ports were in use, whether a web server was already running, and the OS release. Then it installed Caddy from Caddy’s official repository, configured the proxy and made sure ufw allowed web traffic.

It read Caddy’s logs to confirm the Let’s Encrypt certificate, which arrived in about 6 seconds. Finally it tested its own work: HTTPS returned 200, and plain HTTP returned a 308 redirect. The whole task took about two minutes.

To give it a real fault, I ran docker stop demo-app and reloaded the site. Then I asked why it was returning a 502 and to fix it.

In a single command, it checked the container state (Exited (137)) and searched Caddy’s logs, where it found connect: connection refused on port 3000. It restarted the container, confirmed /health and HTTPS were back, and even pointed to my docker stop in the terminal history. It also explained that --restart unless-stopped covers crashes and reboots, but not a manual stop.

A tip it didn’t mention: exit code 137 means Docker had to force-kill the container, because Node running as PID 1 ignores SIGTERM. Add --init to docker run for clean, instant shutdowns.

This was the most impressive answer. ufw already allowed only those three ports, but Agent noticed port 3000 was still reachable from the internet, because Docker-published ports bypass ufw rules.

It recreated the container bound to 127.0.0.1:3000, so the app is only reachable through Caddy, and confirmed with an external port check. It left DNS, time sync and Caddy’s local admin port running, explaining that stopping them would break DNS and time sync.

Then I asked it to reboot the server. First it checked that Docker and Caddy start on boot and that the container’s restart policy was set, then it rebooted. The site came back over HTTPS without any help from me.

Nothing I asked for was destructive, so Agent just got on with it: the firewall change, the container rebuild and the reboot all ran without a confirmation prompt.

The Agent panel says so upfront, noting that terminal commands can run without one. For destructive actions such as reinstalling the OS or restoring a backup, Hostinger’s FAQ says Agent always asks for confirmation first.

One thing worth knowing: to close port 3000, Agent removed and recreated my container. That was harmless for a stateless demo, but a container that keeps data without a volume would lose it. Take a snapshot before big jobs, and keep the panel in view.

Here are the four plans at their Black Friday rates for a 24-month term.

For scale, here’s what my test used. With the Node app, Docker and Caddy all running, KVM 1 had 3.3 GB of its 4 GB RAM still available, and the app container itself used about 65 MB.

So 4 GB is plenty for one or two small apps. Move to 8 GB on KVM 2 once you add Coolify, a database, or n8n with its own Postgres, because those are the services that eat memory.

Finding a cheap VPS got harder in 2026, because memory got expensive. AI data centres are buying up DRAM, and hosts are passing the cost on. In April 2026, Hetzner raised cloud server prices by up to 37%, citing hardware costs, then raised prices again in June. On the same April date, OVHcloud’s entry VPS went from $4.90 to $7.60, a 55% jump. Nobody can promise where VPS prices go next, but the trend this year has been up.

This is how Hostinger’s Black Friday pricing works. You pay upfront for 12 or 24 months, and the 24-month term gives the lowest monthly rate. Your price is fixed for that whole term. After that, it renews at the standard rate.

On KVM 2, for example, you pay $210.96 today (the $8.79/mo rate) for 24 months, and it renews at $14.99/mo after that. Do the maths on the renewal before you commit, not just the headline rate.
